notes.b: Some PE activities are about making something as well as doing it. Artistic activities ask you to craft a performance creatively, rather than simply repeat set movements.
points: Artistic activities give learners creative crafting and performance of activities, so the student acts as a maker of the routine as well as a performer of it.
They involve imaginative combinations of skills, techniques and/or movements, which means the skills are linked in an original way rather than shown one by one.
The combinations are performed in the appropriate style of the event, so a gymnastics routine and a dance each follow the conventions of their own activity.
notes.tip: Written questions use aesthetic activities to test aesthetic and artistic criteria, so be ready to say what makes a combination of movements imaginative and suited to the style of the event.

notes.b: Aesthetic means to do with the beauty and quality of movement. Aesthetic activities are judged on how movement looks and what it expresses, not only on whether a skill was completed.
points: Aesthetic activities give learners the opportunity to demonstrate appreciation of the qualities of movement, such as how smooth, controlled or well shaped it is.
They also show appreciation of the expressive abilities of the performers, meaning how well performers communicate mood or meaning through movement.

Learners demonstrate this by adopting aesthetic criteria (the standards used to judge the quality of movement) when they plan, perform and evaluate the activity, so the criteria are used at all three stages.
notes.tip: Remember the three verbs: plan, perform and evaluate. Aesthetic criteria apply to all three, not only to the performance itself.

notes.b: This area of the course is made up of a short list of activities. You need to know exactly which ones are on it and how this area fits into your choice of activities.
points: The area offers artistic gymnastics, rhythmic gymnastics and dance.
Dance may be in any one of eight styles: contemporary, folk, modern, ballet, jazz, tap, ethnic or traditional.
One activity from this area may be one of the student's three, so a student can choose at most one of these as part of their three activities.

notes.h: Links to compositional elements and criteria
notes.b: Every routine is put together from building blocks and then judged against a set of standards. Knowing both lets you plan a routine and explain why it earns credit.
points: Routines are built from compositional elements (the building blocks used to put a routine together): action, space, dynamics, relationships and choreographic form (the overall structure of the routine or dance).
Routines are judged against aesthetic and artistic criteria: body line, control, fluency, musicality, expression and originality.
Example: a planned change from high to low levels uses the space element, because it uses the performance area in a deliberate way.
Example: a balance held still with a clean finish shows control, because the performer stays steady and ends the movement cleanly.
notes.tip: Written questions on aesthetic activities ask about aesthetic and artistic criteria, compositional elements, methods of analysing choreography and comparing two activities. Learn the two lists so you can name them and link an example to each.

notes.h: Safe practice in gymnastics and dance
notes.b: Gymnastics and dance put demanding stresses on the body, so safe practice is part of the activity and is assessed. Each precaution below is aimed at preventing a particular kind of injury.
points: The warm-up includes mobility work (moving joints through their range) before skills are attempted, so the body is prepared for demanding movements.
Skills are taught through correct progressions, with each simpler step secured before the next is attempted, so a difficult skill is never tried before its basics are safe.
In gymnastics, spotting and supporting (a helper stays close to guide or catch the performer) are used when a skill needs them, which protects the performer if it goes wrong.
Mats are positioned and checked, and apparatus is checked before use, so landings are cushioned and equipment will not fail.
No jewellery is worn and hair is tied back, so nothing catches on equipment or other people or blocks the performer's view.
Dance requires a suitable floor surface, which reduces the risk of slipping and of jarring the joints.
Hydration (drinking enough water) is part of safe practice.
Overuse is avoided to prevent injury, because repeating the same movements too often without rest strains the body.

notes.b: Your practical work is assessed on more than the skills themselves. The assessment also tests what you know about building routines and how safely you work.
points: Assessment covers the listed skills performed within a routine or dance, not skills shown in isolation.
It also covers compositional and choreographic knowledge (how a routine or dance is put together).
Rules of the activity and safe practice are assessed.
Performances are captured on video.
In written exams, aesthetic activities are used to test aesthetic and artistic criteria, compositional elements, methods of analysing choreography and the comparison of two activities.
notes.tip: For the written exam, prepare to apply the criteria and the compositional elements to a routine, to analyse choreography, and to compare two activities.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between artistic and aesthetic activities, giving an example from gymnastics or dance.
questions.model: An artistic activity gives learners creative crafting and performance: they combine skills, techniques and/or movements imaginatively, in the appropriate style of the event. An aesthetic activity gives learners the opportunity to appreciate the qualities of movement and the expressive abilities of performers, and learners use aesthetic criteria to plan, perform and evaluate it. Example from gymnastics: a gymnast who designs a new combination of skills and movements for a floor routine, and performs it in the style of artistic gymnastics, is working in an artistic activity. Example from dance: a learner who watches a classmate's dance and judges its fluency, body line and expression against aesthetic criteria is demonstrating appreciation of the quality of the movement, which is the aesthetic focus.

questions.prompt: Outline three safe-practice measures in gymnastics.
questions.model: First, a warm-up that includes mobility work is completed before any skill is attempted, so the joints and muscles are prepared. Second, correct progressions are followed, with each simpler step secured before a harder one is tried, and spotting and supporting are used where a skill needs them. Third, the mats are positioned and checked and the apparatus is checked before use, and performers wear no jewellery and tie back their hair.
